catalog_quote: Stress is a rather complex phenomenon in /'kesu?/ and a full description falls outside the scope of this paper. We therefore confine ourselves to a few general remarks. The place of the stress is distinctive: /'talomo/ 'he has lost' /ta'lomo/ 'we go, let's go' ... In general the stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word base and remains there in case of suffixation and/or prefixation. …

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.recode_to: Keep penultimate (penultimate stress) and dominant-set membership; strict-set membership is defensible under the 1997 analysis (clitics outside the word) but should carry the stated sub-rule that prefixed monosyllabic roots keep root stress (word-final: meséng, maqrók, dirók) and S&S's final-stressed contracted/expressive items (/a'lan/, /ba?'bak/). If the catalog's 'no rule-level exceptions' test counts clause (c) as a rule-level exception, move to fixed-dominant; otherwise no reclassification.
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: verbatim on S&S 1977 printed p.22 in the PDF we hold (page image checked), locator correct; but the record's own quote/cite/loc/grade fields are blank — the passage sits only in the domain-quote and sources fields. (2) Deciding source: a 1977 structuralist phonology article by a native-speaker linguist, impressionistic; the fuller 1997 Pusat Bahasa grammar by the same author is held and states the rule more strongly ('dapat diramalkan.. suku kedua dari belakang', pp.59, 190) with affixed, reduplicated and compound examples, clitics explicitly unstressed and outside the domain (p.61, 194), and one stated sub-regularity (monosyllabic roots keep stress under prefixation, p.60, 194(c)). Both sources agree on penultimate stress over root+affixes; S&S's 'distinctive' minimal pairs are suffix-vs-enclitic pairs, which the 1997 grammar resolves. No instrumental or later phonological stu
